title: How do we check on baby's health
description:
Learn about the various methods healthcare providers use to monitor your baby's health and development throughout pregnancy.
Please be aware that tests and scans only show part of the picture of your baby's health, your instinct and daily awareness of your baby's movements is just as important. If you have any concerns, even if the scan is normal, please contact your midwife or doctor right away.

contentSections.title: Fundal height measurement
contentSections.content:
The fundal height measurement is a common way that your midwife or doctor may measure how well your baby is growing. To do this they will use a tape measure to measure the distance between your pubic bone and the top of your 'bump' (the uterus or 'fundus').

Plotting this measurement on a chart lets them track the rate of your baby's growth. If this measurement is higher or lower than expected you may be referred for follow up tests such as ultrasound to take a closer look at baby.

contentSections.title: Fetal heart rate
contentSections.content: Monitoring your baby's heart rate during pregnancy helps your midwife/doctor assess your baby's well-being. A normal fetal heart rate typically ranges from 110 to 160 beats per minute – so don't be concerned that their heart is beating faster than yours most of the time! Changes in this heart rate can signal how your baby is coping inside the womb and whether they're getting enough oxygen.

contentSections.title: Clinician/Midwife checks
contentSections.content: Clinician/midwife checks are a common way that your midwife or doctor may check on your baby's health. They will check your baby's heart rate, fundal height, and other things to make sure your baby is growing as expected.

contentSections.title: Ultrasound
contentSections.content:
Ultrasound is a safe and important tool that uses sound waves to create images of your baby in the womb. It helps healthcare providers monitor your baby's development and detect any potential issues throughout pregnancy.

In New Zealand, all pregnant people can have publicly funded ultrasounds at two important times in pregnancy – the end of the first trimester (~12 weeks of gestation), and in the middle of pregnancy (~20 weeks of gestation) . You may also be referred for an ultrasound later in pregnancy to check baby’s health more closely if you are a person who is more likely to have a smaller baby or a complicated pregnancy (for example, if your last baby was small, or you have health conditions like diabetes or high blood pressure), or there is a need to check their growth or health.

Other reasons to have a scan might be to check the baby’s position as birth nears, or to followup any changes seen at the anatomy scan. Our ultrasound tool helps visualise and explain more about what is being measured by ultrasound in pregnancy, and what this can mean.

contentSections.title: Blood pressure
contentSections.content:
Checking blood pressure throughout your pregnancy is important for monitoring disorders such as gestational hypertension or pre-eclampsia.

Gestational hypertension is developed after 20 weeks of pregnancy. In this case, blood pressure readings are typically 140 mmHg / 90 mmHg, which is much higher than normal (120 mmHg / 80 mmHg).

If this persists, you may develop pre-eclampsia, which presents major complications to the health of mum and baby.

contentSections.title: Urine dipstick
contentSections.content:
Regular urine checks with a dipstick can help detect early signs of pre-eclampsia. This is a fast screening tool to test for the presence of protein in urine, which may be an indication of declining kidney health.

Generally, kidneys filter out proteins and prevent them leaking into urine. If protein is present in the screening, you may be asked to collect your urine in a jug over 12-24 hours to determine how much protein is lost. If further testing shows more than 300 mg of protein in urine per day, that may indicate pre-eclampsia.
